name: Nyankpa
catalog_citation: Blench, Roger. 2009. The Nyankpa [= Yeskwa] language of Central Nigeria [Draft circulated for comment; printout May 20, 2009]. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. 32 pp. PDF via the Internet Archive capture 2017-10-13 of rogerblench.info/Language/Nig…
catalog_locator: sec. 3.3 Tones, p. 4 (lines 248-270); sec. 3.1 Vowels p. 2 for vowel length
catalog_quote: 3.3 Tones Nyankpa has three level tones and a rising tone. The basic conventions are as follows; High ʹ Mid Unmarked Low ˋ Rising ˇ Rising tone appears to occur on some short vowels, for example; Slaughter (animal) tɛ̌t ... Toad ŋwǎfɔ̀ There are also sequences of like vowels with two different tones, creating a phonetic rising tone. Some examples are; Who? nyɛɛ̀́ I FUT màá not FUT sèé Such sequences occur principally as a result of morphophonological processes and do not seem to occur in standard vocabulary.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim in the Blench 2009 PDF we hold/txt at sec. 3.3, p.4 (the text layer); 'stress'/'accent' occur nowhere in the 32-pp document. (2) Deciding source: a 2009 draft grammar sketch + wordlist by the only linguist to have worked on the language first-hand; Glottolog's entire descriptive bibliography for yesk1239 is four 'study of one feature' items (two are redrafts of this same sketch, one an Ilorin student essay, one a 43-pp community parts-of-speech booklet); CrossRef has zero Nyankpa/Yeskwa records; no reference grammar, phonology article or instrumental study exists. (3) downloaded now: Gerhardt 2005 (HAAP 3) treats Yeskwa as tonal; four 2011 University of Ilorin long essays recovered from the Internet Archive (including Alabi 'Aspects of Yeskwa phonology', the only dedicated phonology write-up, and Adeyanju = Glottolog 546827) all state H/M/L register tones pl

sources.quote: 'Yeskwa language has three distinct registered tones which are: High, Low, Mid (not graphically marked). Yeskwa also has one contour which is rising tone ... rising tone appears to occur on some short vowels and they are not too common' (2.5); 'Yeskwa like most Bantu languages is a tone language' (4.2); 4.2.4 tone marks singular/plural. 'stress' occurs only in a generic textbook definition of suprasegmentals (line 270); no word stress or accent is described for Yeskwa.
